summary: Cyprus is an EU member but not part of the Schengen Area, so it runs its own national visa policy aligned with the EU visa-free list: EU/EEA citizens enter freely, Schengen-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180 (which do not count against the Schengen allowance), and holders of valid multiple-entry Schengen visas can generally enter without a separate Cypriot visa.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air or sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere in towns and resorts. Keep a little cash for village tavernas, kiosks and rural areas.

safety.text: Cyprus has low crime and is very safe for visitors. The main considerations are summer heat, strong sun, and care around the UN buffer zone — photography of military areas is prohibited.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cyprus travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October offer warm seas without the intense heat of July–August; winters are mild on the coast, with skiing occasionally possible on Mount Olympus in the Troodos.

idp.text: Cyprus is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Cyprus yet.

tips.text: Entering Cyprus through airports or ports in the Turkish-occupied north (e.g. Ercan) is treated as illegal entry by the Republic of Cyprus. Arrive via the south (Larnaca or Paphos). You can then cross to the north and back at recognized checkpoints with your passport.
Cyprus drives on the left, a legacy of British rule. Take extra care at roundabouts and when picking up a rental car, and note that rural roads can be narrow and winding.
Days spent in Cyprus do not count against your Schengen 90/180 allowance — Cyprus is EU but not Schengen — making it a popular stop for travelers resetting their Schengen days.
July and August regularly exceed 35–40°C inland. Plan sightseeing at ancient sites like Kourion and Paphos for early morning, and carry water.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Cyprus?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Nationalities on the EU visa-free list — including the US, UK, Canada and Australia — get 90 days in any 180-day period. Others need a Cypriot national short-stay visa from a Cypriot mission, or can generally enter with a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa.

faq.question: Can I enter Cyprus with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Generally yes — Cyprus accepts valid double- or multiple-entry Schengen visas that have already been used to enter the Schengen Area, without a separate Cypriot visa. Confirm your specific case with a Cypriot mission before travel, as single-entry visas do not qualify.

faq.question: Do days in Cyprus count against the Schengen 90/180 limit?
faq.answer: No. Cyprus is an EU member but not part of the Schengen Area, so time spent there is counted separately from your Schengen allowance. ETIAS will, however, cover Cyprus once it becomes mandatory.

faq.question: Can I visit Northern Cyprus?
faq.answer: Yes, by crossing at recognized checkpoints (such as Ledra Street in Nicosia) with your passport after entering through the south. Arriving directly in the north via Ercan airport or northern ports is considered illegal entry by the Republic of Cyprus and can cause problems, including refusal of entry in the south.

faq.question: Which side of the road does Cyprus drive on?
faq.answer: The left, like the UK, Ireland and Malta. Rental cars are right-hand drive with distinctive red plates, and speed limits are posted in kilometers per hour.
